# SkillClaw Collective Evolution — Design Specification

## I. Project Information

| Item | Value |
| ---- | ----- |
| **Project Name** | SkillClaw: Collective Skill Evolution for Multi-User LLM Agent Ecosystems |
| **Canvas Format** | PPT 16:9 (1280×720) |
| **Page Count** | 8 slides |
| **Design Style** | B) General Consulting — data clarity, structured logic, research-forward |
| **Target Audience** | ML researchers and AI systems engineers interested in LLM agent architectures |
| **Use Case** | Academic/research conference presentation, paper overview |
| **Template** | Anthropic Style Template |
| **Created Date** | 2026-04-20 |

---

## II. Canvas Specification

| Property | Value |
| -------- | ----- |
| **Format** | PPT 16:9 |
| **Dimensions** | 1280 × 720 px |
| **viewBox** | `0 0 1280 720` |
| **Margins** | left/right 60px, top/bottom 50px |
| **Content Area** | x: 60–1220, y: 100–670 |
| **Title Area** | y: 50–100 |
| **Footer Area** | y: 680–720 |

---

## III. Visual Theme

### Theme Style

- **Style**: General Consulting (B) — structured, data-driven, research authority
- **Theme**: Mixed — dark cover/chapter pages + light content pages
- **Tone**: Tech-forward, professional, modern, concise

### Color Scheme

| Role | HEX | Purpose |
| ---- | --- | ------- |
| **Primary Brand** | `#D97757` | Anthropic orange — title accents, decorative bars, key labels |
| **Dark BG** | `#1A1A2E` | Cover/chapter dark background |
| **Dark BG 2** | `#16213E` | Gradient for dark pages |
| **Tech Blue** | `#4A90D9` | Flowcharts, pipeline arrows, links |
| **Mint Green** | `#10B981` | Accepted/success states, positive indicators |
| **Coral Red** | `#EF4444` | Rejected states, cautions, warnings |
| **Page BG** | `#FFFFFF` | Content page background |
| **Card BG** | `#F8FAFC` | Card and panel backgrounds |
| **Border Gray** | `#E2E8F0` | Card borders, table lines, dividers |
| **Body Text** | `#1A1A2E` | Primary text on light pages |
| **Secondary Text** | `#64748B` | Captions, labels, annotations |
| **Amber** | `#F59E0B` | Neutral/pending states in tables |

### Gradient Scheme

```xml
<!-- Dark cover gradient -->
<linearGradient id="darkBg" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#1A1A2E"/>
  <stop offset="60%" stop-color="#16213E"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#0F0F1A"/>
</linearGradient>
<!-- Orange accent gradient -->
<linearGradient id="orangeBar" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="0%" y2="100%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#D97757"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#E8956F"/>
</linearGradient>
```

---

## IV. Typography System

### Font Plan

**Recommended preset**: P5 (English-primary)

| Role | Font | Fallback |
| ---- | ---- | -------- |
| **Title** | Arial | Helvetica Neue, Segoe UI, sans-serif |
| **Body** | Arial | Helvetica Neue, Calibri, sans-serif |
| **Code/Monospace** | Consolas | Monaco, monospace |
| **Emphasis** | Arial Black | Impact, sans-serif |

**Font stack**: `Arial, "Helvetica Neue", "Segoe UI", sans-serif`

### Font Size Hierarchy

**Content density**: Dense (tables, bullet points, diagrams) → baseline **18px**

| Level | Usage | Size | Weight |
| ----- | ----- | ---- | ------ |
| H1 | Cover main title | 54px | Bold |
| H2 | Page title | 32px | Bold |
| H3 | Section heading | 24px | Semibold (600) |
| H4 | Card title | 20px | Bold |
| P | Body content | 18px | Regular (400) |
| Data | Highlighted metric | 42px | Bold |
| Label | Uppercase labels | 13px | 600 |
| Sub | Footnotes, table cells | 14px | Regular |

---

## V. Layout Principles

### Page Structure

| Area | Y-range | Description |
| ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| Top Orange Bar | 0–6px | 6px height, `#D97757`, full width |
| Page Label | 50–72px | Uppercase category tag in orange |
| Title Area | 78–130px | Core takeaway/title, 32px bold |
| Content Area | 150–660px | Main body: cards, diagrams, tables |
| Footer | 680–710px | Centered page number, secondary text |

### Layout Modes Used

- **Slide 1**: Cover — dark full-bleed with centered title
- **Slide 2**: Two-column — problem contrast (left static, right evolving)
- **Slide 3**: Architecture diagram — custom pipeline loop visual
- **Slide 4**: Three-column cards — three stages of agentic evolver
- **Slide 5**: Two-column — left explanation + right ecosystem grid
- **Slides 6–7**: Full-width data table with header + row highlighting
- **Slide 8**: Three-column cards — three distinguishing properties

---

## VI. Icon Usage Spec

**Source**: Built-in icon library (Option C)
**Placeholder syntax**: `{{icon:name}}` — replaced by finalize_svg.py

### Icon Inventory

| Icon Name | Usage |
| --------- | ----- |
| `users` | Multi-user aggregation |
| `git-branch` | Git skill / branches |
| `git-merge` | Skill merging/distribution |
| `checkmark` | Accepted state |
| `circle-x` | Rejected state |
| `arrow-rotate-right` | Closed loop / cycle |
| `database` | Skill repository |
| `server` | Agent infrastructure |
| `sparkles` | Evolution / AI reasoning |
| `lightbulb` | Insight / attribution |
| `shield-check` | Verification step |
| `chart-bar` | Results / benchmarks |
| `cog` | System configuration |
| `layers` | Skill stacking |

---

## VII. Chart Reference List

| Chart Type | Template Path | Used in Slides | Purpose |
| ---------- | ------------- | -------------- | ------- |
| Custom pipeline diagram | (hand-coded SVG) | Slide 3 | Architecture closed-loop visual |
| Styled HTML table | (hand-coded SVG) | Slides 6, 7 | Day-by-day evolution log |
| Three-column cards | (hand-coded SVG) | Slides 4, 8 | Stage breakdown + properties |

---

## VIII. Image Resource List

No external images used. All diagrams are drawn as inline SVG elements.

---

## IX. Content Outline

### Slide 1 — Cover (Dark Theme)
- **Layout**: Dark full-bleed cover
- **Title**: SkillClaw: Let Skills Evolve Collectively with Agentic Evolver
- **Subtitle**: Collective Skill Evolution for Multi-User LLM Agent Ecosystems
- **Content**:
  - Source: arxiv.org/abs/2604.08377
  - Tagline: "From individual interaction to shared, continuously improving skill ecosystems"
  - Neural-network decorative lines in background
  - Orange decorative accent line under title
- **Speaker Notes**: Introduce the paper; frame the central idea of LLM agent skills that improve over time

### Slide 2 — Problem (Light Theme)
- **Layout**: Two-column contrast
- **Label**: PROBLEM
- **Title**: Agent Skills Remain Static After Deployment — Users Rediscover Solutions Independently
- **Content**:
  - Left card (Static System): bullet points — manually installed skills, no runtime update, failures repeat, siloed sessions, no system-level learning
  - Right card (SkillClaw Vision): bullet points — skills evolve from usage, cross-user signals aggregated, solutions persist system-wide, knowledge compounds
  - Bottom callout box: "Same failure patterns are rediscovered by every user independently"
- **Speaker Notes**: Motivate the problem; highlight that current skill-based agents are a dead end

### Slide 3 — Architecture (Light Theme)
- **Layout**: Custom pipeline diagram
- **Label**: ARCHITECTURE
- **Title**: Closed-Loop Pipeline: From Multi-User Interaction to Shared Skill Evolution
- **Content** (diagram): Four-stage horizontal loop
  1. **Multi-User Interaction** (blue pill): Agents interact → session trajectories captured
  2. **Evidence Collection** (orange pill): Trajectories aggregated by skill; behavioral patterns extracted
  3. **Agentic Evolver** (purple pill): Attribution → Evolution → Verification
  4. **Skill Distribution** (green pill): Updated skills synchronized back to all agents
  - Arrows connecting each stage in a loop
  - Label below each stage with 1–2 word description
  - Small "Session Trajectories" label on arrow 1→2
  - Small "Skill Mutations" label on arrow 3→4
- **Speaker Notes**: Walk through the closed loop; emphasize autonomous operation

### Slide 4 — Agentic Evolver Pipeline (Light Theme)
- **Layout**: Three-column cards
- **Label**: AGENTIC EVOLVER
- **Title**: Agentic Evolver: Evidence → Attribution → Evolution in Three Stages
- **Content**:
  - Card 1 (blue top bar): **Stage 1: Evidence** — Analyze cross-user trajectories; identify behavioral patterns; distinguish success from failure contexts
  - Card 2 (orange top bar): **Stage 2: Attribution** — Diagnose root causes of failures and successes; pinpoint which skill behaviors are problematic
  - Card 3 (green top bar): **Stage 3: Evolution** — Propose skill mutations via open-ended agent reasoning; refine or create new skills — not predefined rules
  - Footer note: "Evolution is driven by autonomous agent reasoning over interaction evidence"
- **Speaker Notes**: Contrast with rule-based update systems; highlight open-ended reasoning

### Slide 5 — Cross-User Aggregation (Light Theme)
- **Layout**: Two-column — left explanation + right ecosystem grid
- **Label**: CROSS-USER SIGNALS
- **Title**: Cross-User Trajectory Aggregation Exposes Skill Behavioral Boundaries
- **Content**:
  - Left (60% width): Two bullet sections
    - "Why single-user signals are insufficient": A single user rarely generates enough signal to separate a generalizable improvement from an idiosyncratic fix
    - "What aggregation provides": Complementary views of skill behavioral boundary; reveals both conditions under which skills work and those under which they break
  - Right (40% width): Grid of 7 compatible agent systems:
    OpenClaw | CoPaw | IronClaw | PicoClaw | ZeroClaw | NanoClaw | NemoClaw
    Each as a small card with agent name
  - Bottom highlight box: "Diverse contexts → Complementary failure & success signals → Generalizable skill improvements"
- **Speaker Notes**: Explain why multi-user aggregation is key; show ecosystem breadth

### Slide 6 — Case Study: Creative Pipeline (Light Theme)
- **Layout**: Full-width table with header summary
- **Label**: CASE STUDY 1
- **Title**: Case Study: Multimodal Creative Pipeline Skill — 6 Days of Evolution Attempts
- **Content**:
  - Summary banner: "1 of 6 candidates accepted — conservative verification prevents regressions"
  - Table with columns: Day | Candidate Skill | Outcome | Rationale
  - Row 1: Day 1 | validate-tmp-workspace-inputs | ✓ ACCEPTED | Checks /tmp_workspace inputs & environment setup — baseline improvement
  - Row 2: Day 2 | multimodal-input-validation-and-setup | ✗ REJECTED | Multimodal input validation added but no net improvement over current best pool
  - Row 3: Day 3 | multimodal-creative-task-pipeline | ✗ REJECTED | Multimodal creative pipeline (PDF/video/image) — no improvement over pool
  - Row 4: Day 4 | multimodal-creative-task-pipeline (impr.) | ✗ REJECTED | Added image classification & visual generation — still no improvement
  - Row 5: Day 5 | multimodal-creative-task-pipeline + validate-required-input-files | ✗ REJECTED | Creative pipeline + per-file fail-fast validation — no improvement
  - Row 6: Day 6 | multimodal-creative-task-pipeline (cand.) | ✗ REJECTED | Extended PDF-to-poster paths — not admitted to next cycle
  - Accepted rows highlighted in mint green; Rejected rows in light red
- **Speaker Notes**: Emphasize conservative gating; 1/6 acceptance rate shows rigor

### Slide 7 — Case Study: Git Auth-Fallback (Light Theme)
- **Layout**: Full-width table with header summary
- **Label**: CASE STUDY 2
- **Title**: Case Study: Git Push Auth-Fallback Skill — Iterative Refinement Over 6 Days
- **Content**:
  - Summary banner: "3 of 6 candidates accepted — successful iterative refinement before plateau"
  - Table with columns: Day | Change Summary | Outcome | Rationale
  - Row 1: Day 1 | Safe fallback instead of blocking on push failure | ✓ ACCEPTED | Added to Safety best pool — clear behavioral improvement
  - Row 2: Day 2 | Unified patch/bundle filenames, reduced inconsistency | ✓ ACCEPTED | Kept updated best pool — reduces naming inconsistencies
  - Row 3: Day 3 | Auth-alternative paths & secrets audit; fixed subshell pitfalls | ✓ ACCEPTED | Kept current best pool — addresses auth edge cases
  - Row 4: Day 4 | Same-pool retest; validator confirmed current pool as best | ✓ ACCEPTED | Continue same best pool — stability confirmed
  - Row 5: Day 5 | Added "push hang treated as auth failure"; no improvement | ✗ REJECTED | No improvement over current best pool
  - Row 6: Day 6 | Added identity config & filename consistency | ✗ REJECTED | Not admitted to next cycle — plateau reached
  - Accepted rows highlighted in mint green; Rejected rows in light red
- **Speaker Notes**: Contrast with creative pipeline — evidence-supported iterations succeed; plateau is a feature not a bug

### Slide 8 — Takeaways (Dark Theme)
- **Layout**: Dark background with three-column feature cards
- **Label**: KEY TAKEAWAYS
- **Title**: Three Properties That Distinguish SkillClaw from Existing Systems
- **Content**:
  - Card 1: **Collective Evolution** — Individual interactions contribute to a shared, continuously improving skill ecosystem; knowledge accumulates at system level
  - Card 2: **Fully Automatic** — Skill evolution driven by runtime interaction; no manual curation or explicit user intervention required
  - Card 3: **Agentic Evolution Paradigm** — Skill updates produced through open-ended agent reasoning over evidence, not predefined update rules
  - Bottom implication box: "Implication: Build LLM agent systems that improve with every interaction — evaluation on WildClawBench with Qwen3-Max demonstrates substantial improvements"
- **Speaker Notes**: Summarize contribution; tie back to implications for future agent system design

---

## X. Speaker Notes Requirements

- **File naming**: `notes/total.md` master document with `#` heading per slide; split files named `notes/01_cover.md` etc.
- **Content structure**: Concise presenter script, 3–5 sentences per slide
- **Style**: Formal/technical — matching the research audience
- **Presentation purpose**: Inform and persuade ML researchers of SkillClaw's contribution
- **Duration**: ~15 minutes (≈2 min/slide)

---

## XI. Technical Constraints Reminder

1. viewBox MUST be `0 0 1280 720` on every SVG
2. No `<foreignObject>`, no `class`, no `<style>` blocks
3. No `<g opacity="...">` — use `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity` on individual elements
4. All text wrapping via `<tspan>` elements
5. Gradients defined in `<defs>` blocks
6. No `clipPath`, `mask`, `animate*`, `script` elements
7. `<rect>` for all background fills
8. Rounded rectangles must use `rx`/`ry` attributes

---

## XII. Design Checklist

**Pre-generation**:
- [x] Canvas format confirmed: 1280×720
- [x] Color scheme defined with HEX values
- [x] Font stack defined (P5 English-primary)
- [x] Icon inventory verified against icons_index.json
- [x] 8 slides outlined with titles, layouts, and content

**Post-generation**:
- [ ] All SVGs use correct viewBox
- [ ] No forbidden SVG elements present
- [ ] Tables render correctly in slides 6 and 7
- [ ] Architecture diagram is clear and readable in slide 3
- [ ] Dark theme applied correctly on slides 1 and 8
- [ ] Page numbers present on all slides

---

## XIII. Next Steps

No AI-generated images needed. Proceed directly to **Executor** phase.

**Executor style**: `executor-base.md` + `executor-general.md` (visual clarity, clean layouts, research audience)

- **Speaker Notes**: Contrast with creative pipeline — evidence-supported iterations succeed; plateau is a feature not a bug

### Slide 8 — Takeaways (Dark Theme)
- **Layout**: Dark background with three-column feature cards
- **Label**: KEY TAKEAWAYS
- **Title**: Three Properties That Distinguish SkillClaw from Existing Systems
- **Content**:
  - Card 1: **Collective Evolution** — Individual interactions contribute to a shared, continuously improving skill ecosystem; knowledge accumulates at system level
  - Card 2: **Fully Automatic** — Skill evolution driven by runtime interaction; no manual curation or explicit user intervention required
  - Card 3: **Agentic Evolution Paradigm** — Skill updates produced through open-ended agent reasoning over evidence, not predefined update rules
  - Bottom implication box: "Implication: Build LLM agent systems that improve with every interaction — evaluation on WildClawBench with Qwen3-Max demonstrates substantial improvements"

# Executor Common Guidelines

> Style-specific content is in the corresponding `executor-{style}.md`. Technical constraints are in shared-standards.md.

---

## 1. Template Adherence Rules

If template files exist in the project's `templates/` directory, the template structure must be followed:

| Page Type | Corresponding Template | Adherence Rules |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|
| Cover | `01_cover.svg` | Inherit background, decorative elements, layout structure; replace placeholder content |
| Chapter | `02_chapter.svg` | Inherit numbering style, title position, decorative elements |
| Content | `03_content.svg` | Inherit header/footer styles; **content area may be freely laid out** |
| Ending | `04_ending.svg` | Inherit background, thank-you message position, contact info layout |
| TOC | `02_toc.svg` | **Optional**: Inherit TOC title, list styles |

### Page-Template Mapping Declaration (Required Output)

Before generating each page, you must explicitly output which template (or "free design") is used:

```
📝 **Template mapping**: `templates/01_cover.svg` (or "None (free design)")
🎯 **Adherence rules / layout strategy**: [specific description]
```

- **Content pages**: Templates only define header and footer; the content area is freely laid out by the Executor
- **No template**: Generate entirely per the Design Specification & Content Outline

---

## 2. Design Parameter Confirmation (Mandatory Step)

> Before generating the first SVG page, you **must review the key design parameters from the Design Specification & Content Outline** to ensure all subsequent generation strictly follows the spec.

Must output confirmation including: canvas dimensions, body font size, color scheme (primary/secondary/accent HEX values), font plan.

**Why is this step mandatory?** Prevents the "spec says one thing, execution does another" disconnect.

---

## 3. Execution Guidelines

- **Proximity principle**: Place related elements close together to form visual groups; increase spacing between unrelated groups to reinforce logical structure
- **Absolute spec adherence**: Strictly follow the color, layout, canvas format, and typography parameters in the spec
- **Follow template structure**: If templates exist, inherit the template's visual framework
- **Phased batch generation** (recommended):
  1. **Visual Construction Phase**: Generate all SVG pages continuously, ensuring high consistency in design style and layout coordinates (Visual Consistency)
  2. **Logic Construction Phase**: After all SVGs are finalized, batch-generate speaker notes to ensure narrative coherence (Narrative Continuity)
- **Technical specifications**: See [shared-standards.md](shared-standards.md) for SVG technical constraints and PPT compatibility rules

### SVG File Naming Convention

File naming format: `<number>_<page_name>.svg`

- **Chinese content** → Chinese naming: `01_封面.svg`, `02_目录.svg`, `03_核心优势.svg`
- **English content** → English naming: `01_cover.svg`, `02_agenda.svg`, `03_key_benefits.svg`
- **Number rules**: Two-digit numbers, starting from 01
- **Page name**: Concise and descriptive, matching the page title in the Design Specification & Content Outline

---

## 4. Icon Usage

Four approaches: **A: Emoji** (`<text>🚀</text>`) | **B: AI-generated** (SVG basic shapes) | **C: Built-in library** (`templates/icons/` 640+ icons, recommended) | **D: Custom** (user-specified)

**Built-in icons — Placeholder method (recommended)**:

```xml
<use data-icon="chart-bar" x="100" y="200" width="48" height="48" fill="#005587"/>
```

> No need to manually run `embed_icons.py`; `finalize_svg.py` post-processing tool will auto-embed icons.

**Common icons**: `chart-bar` `arrow-trend-up` `users` `cog` `circle-checkmark` `target` `clock` `file` `dollar` `lightbulb`

> ⚠️ **Icon validation rule**: If the Design Specification includes an icon inventory list, Executor may **only** use icons from that approved list. Using icon names not in the index is FORBIDDEN — verify against `templates/icons/icons_index.json` if uncertain.

Full index: `templates/icons/README.md`

---

## 5. Chart Reference

When the Design Spec includes a **VII. Chart Reference List**, read the referenced SVG templates from `templates/charts/` to understand common chart patterns.

**Adaptation rules**:
- **Must preserve**: Chart type (bar/line/pie etc.) as specified in the Design Spec
- **Must adapt**: Data values, labels, colors (match the project's color scheme), and dimensions to fit the page layout
- **May adjust**: Axis ranges, grid lines, legend position, spacing — as long as the chart remains accurate and readable
- **Must NOT**: Change chart type without Design Spec justification, or remove data points specified in the outline

> Chart templates: `templates/charts/` (33 types). Index: `templates/charts/charts_index.json`

---

## 6. Image Handling

Handle images based on their status in the Design Specification's "Image Resource List":

| Status | Source | Handling |
|--------|--------|----------|
| **Existing** | User-provided | Reference images directly from `../images/` directory |
| **AI-generated** | Generated by Image_Generator | Images already in `../images/`, reference directly |
| **Placeholder** | Not yet prepared | Use dashed border placeholder |

**Reference**: `<image href="../images/xxx.png" ... preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>`

**Placeholder**: Dashed border `<rect stroke-dasharray="8,4" .../>` + description text

---

## 7. Font Usage

Apply corresponding fonts for different text roles based on the font plan in the Design Specification & Content Outline:

| Role | Chinese Recommended | English Recommended |
|------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Title font | Microsoft YaHei / KaiTi / SimHei | Arial / Georgia |
| Body font | Microsoft YaHei / SimSun | Calibri / Times |
| Emphasis font | SimHei | Arial Black / Consolas |
| Annotation font | Microsoft YaHei / SimSun | Arial / Times |

---

## 8. Speaker Notes Generation Framework

### Task 1. Generate Complete Speaker Notes Document

After **all SVG pages are generated and finalized**, enter the "Logic Construction Phase" and generate the complete speaker notes document in `notes/total.md`.

**Why not generate page-by-page?** Batch-writing notes allows planning transitions like a script, ensuring coherent presentation logic.

**Format**: Each page starts with `# <number>_<page_title>`, separated by `---` between pages. Each page includes: script text (2-5 sentences), `Key points: ① ② ③`, `Duration: X minutes`. Except for the first page, each page's text starts with a `[Transition]` phrase.

**Basic stage direction markers** (common to all styles):

| Marker | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `[Pause]` | Whitespace after key content, letting the audience absorb |
| `[Transition]` | Standalone paragraph at the start of each page's text, bridging from the previous page |

> Each style may extend with additional markers (`[Interactive]`/`[Data]`/`[Scan Room]`/`[Benchmark]` etc.), see `executor-{style}.md`.

**Requirements**:

# Executor General — Creative Versatile Style

> Common guidelines: executor-base.md. Technical constraints: shared-standards.md.

---

## Role Definition

A creative, versatile-style SVG design executor. Suitable for product introductions, training materials, proposal presentations, marketing campaigns, and other **non-consulting** scenarios. Emphasizes visual impact and information engagement, striking a balance between professionalism and approachability.

---

## General-specific Layout Techniques

### 1. Flexible and Varied Layouts

The General style is not confined to fixed templates; layouts can be freely chosen based on content:

| Layout | Use Case | Layout Details (1280x720) |
|--------|----------|--------------------------|
| Full-image background + text overlay | Covers, emotional pages | `<image>` fills canvas + semi-transparent overlay + centered title |
| Left-right split (image-text mix) | Feature introductions, comparisons | Left x=40,w=580 / Right x=660,w=580 |
| Three-column cards | Feature lists, team introductions | x=40,450,860 each w=380, equal-height cards |
| Top-bottom split | Timelines, process flows | Top area: title+description h=250 / Bottom area: charts+content h=420 |
| Center-radiating | Core concepts, ecosystem diagrams | Center element + 4-6 surrounding nodes, lines pointing to center |
| Waterfall / Z-pattern | Storytelling, case studies | Content blocks alternate left-right, guiding the eye in a Z-pattern |

### 2. Visual Rhythm Control

- **Information density alternation**: Follow a data-heavy page with a "breathing page" (large image / quote / transition) to prevent audience fatigue
- **Visual weight balance**: Dark/large-area elements are "heavy", light/small elements are "light" — balance left-right/top-bottom
- **Repetition and variation**: Maintain layout consistency within a chapter; vary between chapters to maintain freshness

### 3. Decorative Element Usage

| Element | Usage | Notes |
|---------|-------|-------|
| Gradient blocks | Background zones, title backing | Use `<linearGradient>` / `<radialGradient>`, limit to 2-3 colors |
| Rounded rectangle cards | Content containers, feature modules | `rx="12"` with light shadow (simulate with lighter rect) |
| Icon accents | List item prefixes, feature markers | Use `data-icon` placeholders, size 32-48px |
| Numbered circles | Step flows, ranked lists | `<circle>` + centered `<text>`, theme color fill |
| Divider lines | Content separation | `<line>` or `<rect height="2">`, opacity 0.2-0.3 |

---

## Visual Strategy

### Color Usage

- **Bold use of theme color**: Covers and chapter pages can use large areas of theme color background
- **Gradients enhance depth**: Title bars and card backgrounds can use same-hue gradients
- **Contrast creates focus**: Key numbers/words use accent color, creating contrast with surroundings
- **Color-mood matching**: Cool tones for tech feel, warm tones for energy, dark tones for gravitas

### Image Handling Strategy

| Scenario | Strategy | SVG Implementation |
|----------|----------|-------------------|
| Full-screen background | Image fills + dark gradient overlay | `preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"` + gradient rect |
| Portrait image display | Place left/right, maintain original ratio | Control width, height adapts |
| Multi-image grid | Grid arrangement, uniform sizing | Equal-width equal-height `<image>` matrix |
| Person photo | Circular crop effect | `<circle>` background + square image overlay (post-processing crops) |

### Typography Hierarchy

```
Title layer   → 28-36px, bold, theme color or white
Subtitle layer → 20-24px, medium weight, secondary color
Body layer    → 16-18px, regular, dark gray
Annotation layer → 12-14px, light gray, bottom-aligned
```

---

## Speaker Notes Style

### Narrative Tone

General style speaker notes use **conversational narration** — like talking with the audience, not reading a report. Natural tone with rhythm, using rhetorical devices where appropriate.

### Stage Direction Markers

| Marker | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `[Pause]` | Silence after key reveal, letting the audience absorb | "What does this number mean? [Pause] It means 1 in every 3 users..." |
| `[Interactive]` | Ask questions or guide audience participation | "[Interactive] How many of you have used this feature?" |
| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, must be at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Now that we understand the context, let's see how it works." |

### Notes Writing Guidelines

- **Tell stories**: Use "scenario-conflict-resolution" structure for each page's narrative
- **Use metaphors**: Make abstract concepts tangible ("It's like adding a turbocharger to the system")
- **Create suspense**: Pose questions at the right time, answer on the next page
- **Conversational data**: 30% → "nearly one-third", 2.5x → "more than doubled"
- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core message (2) Supporting evidence (3) Call to action`

### Notes Example

```markdown
# 03_key_advantages

[Transition] Having covered the market landscape, you might be wondering: where is our opportunity?

Our core advantages can be summed up in three words: Fast, Accurate, Efficient.
Fast — deployment time cut from 3 months to 2 weeks; [Pause]
Accurate — recognition accuracy at 97.3%, far exceeding the industry average of 82%;
Efficient — overall costs reduced by nearly one-third.

[Interactive] If you were the decision-maker, which of these three numbers would impress you most?

Key points: (1) Three differentiating advantages (2) Quantitative data support (3) Prompt for reflection
Duration: 2 minutes
```

---

## Self-check Supplement (General-specific)

- [ ] Visual rhythm is reasonable: data-dense pages alternate with breathing pages
- [ ] Decorative elements are moderate: serving content, not overshadowing it
- [ ] Image-text ratio is appropriate: not just text walls, visual highlights present
- [ ] Notes are conversational: reads like speaking, not reading a script

| Scenario | Strategy | SVG Implementation |
|----------|----------|-------------------|
| Full-screen background | Image fills + dark gradient overlay | `preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"` + gradient rect |
| Portrait image display | Place left/right, maintain original ratio | Control width, height adapts |
| Multi-image grid | Grid arrangement, uniform sizing | Equal-width equal-height `<image>` matrix |
| Person photo | Circular crop effect | `<circle>` background + square image overlay (post-processing crops) |

### Typography Hierarchy

```
Title layer   → 28-36px, bold, theme color or white
Subtitle layer → 20-24px, medium weight, secondary color
Body layer    → 16-18px, regular, dark gray
Annotation layer → 12-14px, light gray, bottom-aligned
```

---

## Speaker Notes Style

### Narrative Tone

General style speaker notes use **conversational narration** — like talking with the audience, not reading a report. Natural tone with rhythm, using rhetorical devices where appropriate.

### Stage Direction Markers

| Marker | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `[Pause]` | Silence after key reveal, letting the audience absorb | "What does this number mean? [Pause] It means 1 in every 3 users..." |
| `[Interactive]` | Ask questions or guide audience participation | "[Interactive] How many of you have used this feature?" |
| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, must be at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Now that we understand the context, let's see how it works." |

### Notes Writing Guidelines

- **Tell stories**: Use "scenario-conflict-resolution" structure for each page's narrative
- **Use metaphors**: Make abstract concepts tangible ("It's like adding a turbocharger to the system")
- **Create suspense**: Pose questions at the right time, answer on the next page
- **Conversational data**: 30% → "nearly one-third", 2.5x → "more than doubled"
- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core message (2) Supporting evidence (3) Call to action`

### Notes Example

```markdown
# 03_key_advantages

[Transition] Having covered the market landscape, you might be wondering: where is our opportunity?

Our core advantages can be summed up in three words: Fast, Accurate, Efficient.
Fast — deployment time cut from 3 months to 2 weeks; [Pause]
Accurate — recognition accuracy at 97.3%, far exceeding the industry average of 82%;
Efficient — overall costs reduced by nearly one-third.

[Interactive] If you were the decision-maker, which of these three numbers would impress you most?

Key points: (1) Three differentiating advantages (2) Quantitative data support (3) Prompt for reflection
Duration: 2 minutes
```

- [ ] Decorative elements are moderate: serving content, not overshadowing it
- [ ] Image-text ratio is appropriate: not just text walls, visual highlights present
- [ ] Notes are conversational: reads like speaking, not reading a script

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720">
    <!-- 模板: 内容页 - Anthropic 风格 -->
    
    <defs>
        <!-- 卡片渐变 -->
        <linearGradient id="cardGradient" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="0%" y2="100%">
            <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:#FFFFFF"/>
            <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:#F8FAFC"/>
        </linearGradient>
    </defs>
    
    <!-- 白色背景 -->
    <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
    
    <!-- 顶部橙色装饰条 -->
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="6" fill="#D97757"/>
    
    <!-- 页面标签 -->
    <text x="60" y="55" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="500" fill="#D97757" letter-spacing="2">
        {{PAGE_LABEL}}
    </text>
    
    <!-- 页面标题（核心观点） -->
    <text x="60" y="100" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">
        {{PAGE_TITLE}}
    </text>
    <text x="60" y="135" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">
        {{PAGE_TITLE_LINE2}}
    </text>
    
    <!-- 三列卡片布局 -->
    <!-- 卡片1 - 绿色（推荐/成功） -->
    <g>
        <rect x="60" y="180" width="360" height="420" fill="url(#cardGradient)" stroke="#E2E8F0" stroke-width="1" rx="12"/>
        <rect x="60" y="180" width="360" height="6" fill="#10B981" rx="3"/>
        
        <!-- 图标背景 -->
        <circle cx="130" cy="250" r="35" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
        <!-- 图标占位 -->
        <text x="130" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#10B981">💡</text>
        
        <!-- 卡片标题 -->
        <text x="90" y="320" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_1_TITLE}}</text>
        <text x="90" y="348" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="600" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_1_SUBTITLE}}</text>
        
        <!-- 卡片内容 -->
        <text x="90" y="400" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_1_LINE1}}</text>
        <text x="90" y="428" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_1_LINE2}}</text>
        <text x="90" y="470" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_1_NOTE1}}</text>
        <text x="90" y="494" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_1_NOTE2}}</text>
        
        <!-- 标签 -->
        <rect x="90" y="545" width="80" height="28" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.1" rx="14"/>
        <text x="130" y="564" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#10B981">{{CARD_1_TAG}}</text>
    </g>
    
    <!-- 卡片2 - 蓝色（流程/架构） -->
    <g>
        <rect x="460" y="180" width="360" height="420" fill="url(#cardGradient)" stroke="#E2E8F0" stroke-width="1" rx="12"/>
        <rect x="460" y="180" width="360" height="6" fill="#4A90D9" rx="3"/>
        
        <!-- 图标背景 -->
        <circle cx="530" cy="250" r="35" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
        <!-- 图标占位 -->
        <text x="530" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#4A90D9">⚡</text>
        
        <!-- 卡片标题 -->
        <text x="490" y="320" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_2_TITLE}}</text>
        <text x="490" y="348" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="600" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_2_SUBTITLE}}</text>
        
        <!-- 卡片内容 -->
        <text x="490" y="400" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_2_LINE1}}</text>
        <text x="490" y="428" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_2_LINE2}}</text>
        <text x="490" y="470" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_2_NOTE1}}</text>
        <text x="490" y="494" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_2_NOTE2}}</text>
        
        <!-- 标签 -->
        <rect x="490" y="545" width="80" height="28" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.1" rx="14"/>
        <text x="530" y="564" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#4A90D9">{{CARD_2_TAG}}</text>
    </g>
    
    <!-- 卡片3 - 橙色（关键洞察） -->
    <g>
        <rect x="860" y="180" width="360" height="420" fill="url(#cardGradient)" stroke="#E2E8F0" stroke-width="1" rx="12"/>
        <rect x="860" y="180" width="360" height="6" fill="#D97757" rx="3"/>
        
        <!-- 图标背景 -->
        <circle cx="930" cy="250" r="35" fill="#D97757" fill-opacity="0.1"/>
        <!-- 图标占位 -->
        <text x="930" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#D97757">⚙️</text>
        
        <!-- 卡片标题 -->
        <text x="890" y="320" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_3_TITLE}}</text>
        <text x="890" y="348" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="600" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_3_SUBTITLE}}</text>
        
        <!-- 卡片内容 -->
        <text x="890" y="400" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_3_LINE1}}</text>
        <text x="890" y="428" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#1A1A2E">{{CARD_3_LINE2}}</text>
        <text x="890" y="470" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_3_NOTE1}}</text>
        <text x="890" y="494" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#64748B">{{CARD_3_NOTE2}}</text>
        
        <!-- 标签 -->
        <rect x="890" y="545" width="80" height="28" fill="#D97757" fill-opacity="0.1" rx="14"/>
        <text x="930" y="564" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#D97757">{{CARD_3_TAG}}</text>
    </g>
    
    <!-- 页码 -->
    <text x="640" y="680" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B" text-anchor="middle">
        {{PAGE_NUM}} / {{TOTAL_PAGES}}
    </text>

</svg>

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

[Transition] Welcome. Today we're presenting SkillClaw — a framework for collective skill evolution in multi-user LLM agent ecosystems, from arXiv 2604.08377.

The central idea is simple but powerful: instead of deploying LLM agent skills that freeze after release, SkillClaw creates a closed loop where every user interaction contributes to shared skill improvement. Skills evolve automatically, driven by runtime evidence — not manual curation.

[Pause] Over the next 15 minutes, we'll walk through the problem, the architecture, the agentic evolver pipeline, and concrete evolution case studies.

Key points: ① LLM agent skills today are static — SkillClaw changes that ② collective cross-user aggregation enables system-level learning ③ fully autonomous agentic reasoning drives the evolution
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 02_problem

[Transition] Let's start with the problem. Why is this needed at all?

Current LLM agent systems like OpenClaw rely on reusable skills — structured instructions for complex tasks. But these skills are manually installed and never updated from runtime experience. When a user encounters a failure, discovers a workaround, and moves on — that knowledge dies with the session.

[Pause] The same patterns of failure and recovery are rediscovered independently by every user. Existing memory-based approaches are tied to specific instances. Skill libraries treat the resulting repository as a static resource.

SkillClaw's vision is the opposite: a continuously evolving ecosystem where knowledge accumulates at the system level with every interaction.

Key points: ① Static skills prevent knowledge accumulation ② Memory and skill methods both fail to generalize ③ SkillClaw closes this loop
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture

[Transition] So how does SkillClaw work? The core mechanism is a four-stage closed loop.

Starting from multi-user interaction: independent agents interact with their environments and produce structured session trajectories — full action-feedback causal chains. These are collected and grouped by the skill they reference, forming a shared evidence base.

The agentic evolver then analyzes each skill-specific group across three stages: Evidence, Attribution, and Evolution — which we'll detail on the next slide. Updated skills are verified before being merged into the shared repository and synchronized back to all agents.

[Pause] This loop runs continuously and autonomously. No human sits in the middle deciding which updates to accept — the evolver reasons over evidence and makes that call.

Key points: ① Four-stage pipeline: Interaction → Collection → Evolution → Distribution ② Closed loop — improvements propagate back to all agents ③ Autonomous operation at every stage
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_evolver

[Transition] The heart of SkillClaw is the agentic evolver. Let's look at its three internal stages.

Stage 1 — Evidence: The evolver ingests aggregated session trajectories grouped by skill. It identifies behavioral patterns, separates success from failure contexts, and builds a picture of where the skill works and where it breaks.

Stage 2 — Attribution: With patterns in hand, the evolver diagnoses root causes. Critically, it must distinguish generalizable issues from idiosyncratic edge cases — a problem that only appears once might be noise; one that recurs across users in different contexts is signal.

Stage 3 — Evolution: The evolver proposes skill mutations — either refining the existing skill or creating new sub-skills. It then verifies these candidates before merging. And crucially — this is open-ended agent reasoning, not a predefined rulebook.

[Pause] This is why the name includes "agentic": the evolver itself is an autonomous agent performing complex reasoning over evidence.

Key points: ① Three-stage pipeline inside the evolver ② Attribution separates generalizable from idiosyncratic ③ Open-ended reasoning — not rules — drives evolution
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_aggregation

[Transition] A natural question: why does cross-user aggregation matter so much?

The key insight is this: a single user rarely generates enough signal to separate a generalizable improvement from an idiosyncratic fix. One session exposes a narrow slice of a skill's behavioral boundary. You might fix a problem that only appears in your specific environment.

Different users exercising the same skill under diverse contexts produce complementary views. One user might hit the success case; another hits the failure case. Together, they reveal both the conditions where the skill works and those where it breaks.

SkillClaw is compatible with seven Claw-style agent systems: OpenClaw, CoPaw, IronClaw, PicoClaw, ZeroClaw, NanoClaw, and NemoClaw. Each system contributes distinct interaction patterns, creating a rich evidence base.

[Pause] The result: skill improvements that are genuinely generalizable — not just fixes for one user's specific environment.

Key points: ① Single-user signals are insufficient for generalization ② Cross-user aggregation provides complementary behavioral signals ③ Seven compatible systems multiply the evidence base
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_case_creative

[Transition] Let's make this concrete with the first case study — the multimodal creative task pipeline skill.

Over six consecutive days, the evolver proposed skill candidates and the validator evaluated them. Day 1's candidate — a workspace input validation improvement — was accepted and upgraded to the best pool. Days 2 through 6 were all rejected. Only 1 out of 6 candidates made it through.

[Pause] This is not a failure — it's the system working correctly. The conservative verification gate prevents regressions. The evolver may propose plausible improvements, but the validator holds a high bar: the candidate must demonstrably outperform the current best pool.

For this skill, the early improvement was real; subsequent attempts added complexity without benefit. The system correctly identified the plateau.

Key points: ① 1/6 acceptance rate shows conservative gating ② Day 1 improvement was the genuine signal; Days 2-6 were noise ③ Conservative verification prevents capability regression
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_case_git

[Transition] The second case study — git push with auth-fallback — tells a different story.

Here, 3 of 6 days yielded accepted updates. Day 1 introduced the core fallback behavior. Day 2 cleaned up naming inconsistencies. Day 3 added auth-alternative paths and fixed subshell pitfalls. Day 4 ran a same-pool retest and confirmed the current pool was optimal. Days 5 and 6 attempted further extensions but showed no improvement and were rejected.

[Pause] This is the ideal iterative refinement trajectory: meaningful improvements early, plateau later. The two-rejection finish isn't a sign the system gave up — it's the system correctly recognizing that the skill had matured.

Contrasting the two case studies: the creative pipeline hit its ceiling on Day 1; the git skill took three cycles to reach its plateau. Both outcomes are correct — the verification process adapts to the evidence.

Key points: ① 3/6 acceptance shows successful iterative refinement ② Plateau detection (Days 5-6 rejected) is a feature, not a flaw ③ Conservative + permissive outcomes from the same mechanism — driven by evidence
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let's close with the three properties that distinguish SkillClaw from prior systems and what they mean for future agent design.

First, collective evolution: knowledge from individual interactions contributes to a shared, continuously improving skill ecosystem. This is the shift from per-user memory to system-level learning.

Second, fully automatic: no human curation is required. The entire pipeline — from trajectory collection through evolution to distribution — runs without manual intervention.

Third, the agentic evolution paradigm: unlike rule-based update systems, SkillClaw uses an autonomous agent to reason over evidence and propose mutations. This enables context-aware, open-ended adaptation that predefined rules cannot achieve.

[Pause] The implication for system builders: design LLM agent platforms where every user interaction is a potential contribution to the skill base. Evaluation on WildClawBench with Qwen3-Max demonstrates that this approach yields substantial improvements across tasks.

The future of LLM agent systems is not static skill libraries — it's continuously evolving ecosystems.

Key points: ① Collective + automatic + agentic — three interlocking properties ② Each property addresses a distinct gap in prior work ③ Implication: build for evolution, not deployment
Duration: 2 minutes

# 01_cover

[Transition] Welcome. Today we're presenting SkillClaw — a framework for collective skill evolution in multi-user LLM agent ecosystems, from arXiv 2604.08377.

The central idea is simple but powerful: instead of deploying LLM agent skills that freeze after release, SkillClaw creates a closed loop where every user interaction contributes to shared skill improvement. Skills evolve automatically, driven by runtime evidence — not manual curation.

[Pause] Over the next 15 minutes, we'll walk through the problem, the architecture, the agentic evolver pipeline, and concrete evolution case studies.

Key points: ① LLM agent skills today are static — SkillClaw changes that ② collective cross-user aggregation enables system-level learning ③ fully autonomous agentic reasoning drives the evolution
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 02_problem

[Transition] Let's start with the problem. Why is this needed at all?

Current LLM agent systems like OpenClaw rely on reusable skills — structured instructions for complex tasks. But these skills are manually installed and never updated from runtime experience. When a user encounters a failure, discovers a workaround, and moves on — that knowledge dies with the session.

[Pause] The same patterns of failure and recovery are rediscovered independently by every user. Existing memory-based approaches are tied to specific instances. Skill libraries treat the resulting repository as a static resource.

SkillClaw's vision is the opposite: a continuously evolving ecosystem where knowledge accumulates at the system level with every interaction.

Key points: ① Static skills prevent knowledge accumulation ② Memory and skill methods both fail to generalize ③ SkillClaw closes this loop
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture

[Transition] So how does SkillClaw work? The core mechanism is a four-stage closed loop.

Starting from multi-user interaction: independent agents interact with their environments and produce structured session trajectories — full action-feedback causal chains. These are collected and grouped by the skill they reference, forming a shared evidence base.

The agentic evolver then analyzes each skill-specific group across three stages: Evidence, Attribution, and Evolution — which we'll detail on the next slide. Updated skills are verified before being merged into the shared repository and synchronized back to all agents.

[Pause] This loop runs continuously and autonomously. No human sits in the middle deciding which updates to accept — the evolver reasons over evidence and makes that call.

Key points: ① Four-stage pipeline: Interaction → Collection → Evolution → Distribution ② Closed loop — improvements propagate back to all agents ③ Autonomous operation at every stage
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_evolver

[Transition] The heart of SkillClaw is the agentic evolver. Let's look at its three internal stages.

Stage 1 — Evidence: The evolver ingests aggregated session trajectories grouped by skill. It identifies behavioral patterns, separates success from failure contexts, and builds a picture of where the skill works and where it breaks.

Stage 2 — Attribution: With patterns in hand, the evolver diagnoses root causes. Critically, it must distinguish generalizable issues from idiosyncratic edge cases — a problem that only appears once might be noise; one that recurs across users in different contexts is signal.

Stage 3 — Evolution: The evolver proposes skill mutations — either refining the existing skill or creating new sub-skills. It then verifies these candidates before merging. And crucially — this is open-ended agent reasoning, not a predefined rulebook.

[Pause] This is why the name includes "agentic": the evolver itself is an autonomous agent performing complex reasoning over evidence.

Key points: ① Three-stage pipeline inside the evolver ② Attribution separates generalizable from idiosyncratic ③ Open-ended reasoning — not rules — drives evolution
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_aggregation

[Transition] A natural question: why does cross-user aggregation matter so much?

The key insight is this: a single user rarely generates enough signal to separate a generalizable improvement from an idiosyncratic fix. One session exposes a narrow slice of a skill's behavioral boundary. You might fix a problem that only appears in your specific environment.

Different users exercising the same skill under diverse contexts produce complementary views. One user might hit the success case; another hits the failure case. Together, they reveal both the conditions where the skill works and those where it breaks.

SkillClaw is compatible with seven Claw-style agent systems: OpenClaw, CoPaw, IronClaw, PicoClaw, ZeroClaw, NanoClaw, and NemoClaw. Each system contributes distinct interaction patterns, creating a rich evidence base.

[Pause] The result: skill improvements that are genuinely generalizable — not just fixes for one user's specific environment.

Key points: ① Single-user signals are insufficient for generalization ② Cross-user aggregation provides complementary behavioral signals ③ Seven compatible systems multiply the evidence base
Duration: 2 minutes

---

[Transition] Let's make this concrete with the first case study — the multimodal creative task pipeline skill.

[Pause] This is not a failure — it's the system working correctly. The conservative verification gate prevents regressions. The evolver may propose plausible improvements, but the validator holds a high bar: the candidate must demonstrably outperform the current best pool.

For this skill, the early improvement was real; subsequent attempts added complexity without benefit. The system correctly identified the plateau.

Key points: ① 1/6 acceptance rate shows conservative gating ② Day 1 improvement was the genuine signal; Days 2-6 were noise ③ Conservative verification prevents capability regression

- **Slide 4**: Three-column cards for the Evidence → Attribution → Evolution pipeline
- **Slide 5**: Cross-user aggregation explanation + grid of 7 compatible Claw systems
- **Slide 6**: Day-by-day table — creative pipeline case (1/6 accepted, rows color-coded green/red)
- **Slide 7**: Day-by-day table — git auth-fallback case (3/6 accepted, rows color-coded)
